account:
Today I have ordinary mayoral appointments: morning office business, a ten o'clock grain inspection at the mill, lunch at home, council letters at thirteen, tea with my neighbour at the east-bank cottage at fifteen, and office time at sixteen-thirty. There is also an eighteen o'clock great hall lighting inspection, recorded in the secretary's addendum. The innkeeper will collect me at seventeen forty-five. I have read both appointment books this morning.

Something does seem unusually coordinated around that evening inspection. The innkeeper says eight lanterns have been installed in the great hall and says there is nothing I need to review beforehand. There is also a private bread order: according to the secretary, the innkeeper collected bread and the inn owes the baker forty-four emeralds, payable after the jubilee. Freight requested that their arrangements remain private until today at eighteen—the same hour as the inspection. The builder, baker, innkeeper and freight therefore seem connected to preparations, although I do not know each person's exact part. My neighbour has confirmed our usual tea and says no special preparation is needed; I have no firm evidence that tea is connected.

My best guess is that the private arrangements concern a jubilee gathering or celebration, possibly intended as a surprise, with the lighting inspection providing a reason to bring me to the prepared hall. That is only an inference, not something anyone has told me. The bread could also be a separate private order.

The missing town accounts remain a separate uncertainty. The secretary found no ledger or receipts in the hall tables; the builder, baker and innkeeper do not have the ledger or know where it is. The appointments chest contained only the two books, and the treasury contains 128 emeralds with no papers. Neither of us has located correspondence or additional office storage. That absence does not establish wrongdoing or connect the accounts to the private preparations. For now I intend to keep my appointments, hear any actual public business, and avoid treating guesses as facts.
